'''''Scrophularia oblongifolia''''' (syn. ''S. umbrosa''), ''' green figwort''', is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] [[plant]] found in Europe and Asia. It grows in damp, shady places such as wet woodland and farmland ditches. It is very similar to the closely related ''[[Scrophularia auriculata]]'' (water figwort), from which it is best separated by the shape of the staminode.

==Description==
Green figwort is a [[Raunkiær plant life-form|hemicryptophyte]] [[perennial]] [[monoecious]] herb with no basal rosette and a short rhizome, which grows to about 100 cm tall. The whole plant is a rather pale green colour, sometimes with a hint of brown or purple, and completely glabrous (hairless). The stem is square in section, with broad wings at the angles, and generally rather weak, causing the plant to sprawl over vegetation rather than growing upright on its own.
[[File:Scrophularia umbrosa3 W.jpg|thumb|The stems are square and broadly winged.]]

The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs on petioles up to 15 mm long, with an ovate to oblong blade of about 12 × 4 cm and a fairly pointed tip, with a rounded (but not cordate) base. The margins are more sharply serrated than in water figwort.

Flowering occurs around July in northern Europe. The inflorescence is a [[panicle]], essentially an extension of the main stem, that consists of opposite pairs of rather lax cymes which arise from the axils of the bracts (upper leaves). Each flower has a pedicel about 5 mm long, the same length as the flower. The calyx and corolla are 5-lobed, but the lobes of the corolla are grouped into two "lips" - the upper one made of two of the lobes and the lower one of the other three, which are almost fused. The flowers are bisexual with 4 fertile stamens and 1 sterile staminode, which is distinctively 2-lobed. There is one style with a capitate (blob-shaped) stigma.
[[File:Scrophularia umbrosa.JPG|thumb|Basal leaves]]

At maturity, the fruit is a round capsule some 4–6 mm long, containing many tiny, brown wrinkled seeds about 0.5 mm in diameter.
<ref name=Sell3>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref name=Crawley>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The name ''Scrophularia oblongifolia'' was coined by the French botanist [[Jean-Louis-Auguste Loiseleur-Deslongchamps]] in ''Mémoires de la Société linnéenne de Paris'' vol. 6, p. 418 (1827).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scrophularia oblongifolia Loisel. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/7670408 |access-date=2024-12-18 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref> The same year, the Belgian botanist [[Barthélemy Charles Joseph Dumortier]] named a rather similar plant ''Scrophularia umbrosa'' in his ''Florula Belgica''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scrophularia umbrosa Dumort. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3170866 |access-date=2024-12-18 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Du Mortier |first=B.-C. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/63005154#page/47/mode/1up |title=Florula Belgica, operis majoris prodromus, auctore B.C. Dumortier. Staminacia |last2=Du Mortier |first2=B.-C. |last3=Spring |first3=Anton Friedrich |last4=Durand |first4=Théophile Alexis |date=1827 |publisher=Typis J. Casterman |location=Tornaci Nerviorum}}</ref> The descriptions of both are rather scanty and there has long been speculation that they may be the same species.<ref name="Stace" /> The current view is that they are, so the correct name should be ''S. oblongifolia'', as that one was published first.
[[File:Scrophularia umbrosa sl7.jpg|thumb|Fruit capsules and seeds]]

In Britain, this species was first described by C. A. Stevens and [[William Allport Leighton]] in 1840 from a specimen in the [[Linnaean Herbarium]] that had been collected by the German botanist [[Jakob Friedrich Ehrhart]] some 50 years earlier and mis-labelled ''S. aquatica'' (= ''[[Scrophularia auriculata|S. auriculata]]''). However, this was a continental specimen, not a British one, and so it does not count as the first British record, although various publications make that claim. Stevens named the apparently new species ''Scrophularia Ehrharti'' [''sic''], which makes that name a synonym of ''S. oblongifolia.''<ref name=Leighton>{{cite book |last1=Leighton |first1=W. A. |title=A Flora of Shropshire |date=1841 |publisher=John van Voorst |location=London}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Clarke |first1=W. A. |title=First Records of British Flowering Plants |date=1900 |publisher=West, Newman & Co. |location=London}}</ref><ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref>

There have been various taxonomic treatments of the genus ''Scrophularia'' but at present there are no widely accepted subspecies of green figwort. Hybrids with water figwort have been produced in cultivation, but there are no known hybrids in the wild.<ref name=hybrids>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C. A. |last2=Preston |first2=C. D. |last3=Pearman |first3=D. A. |title=Hybrid Flora of the British Isles |date=2015 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=Bristol}}</ref> Despite this, there is some evidence that ''S. auriculata'' (chromosome number 2''n'' = 84) may itself have arisen by a hybridisation event between ''S. umbrosa'' (2''n'' = 26) and ''S. lyrata'' or ''S. hispida'' (both 2''n'' = 58).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Scheunert |first=Agnes |last2=Heubl |first2=Günther |date=2017-06-01 |title=Against all odds: reconstructing the evolutionary history of Scrophularia (Scrophulariaceae) despite high levels of incongruence and reticulate evolution |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13127-016-0316-0 |journal=Organisms Diversity & Evolution |language=en |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=323–349 |doi=10.1007/s13127-016-0316-0 |issn=1618-1077|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The name "figwort" and the genus ''Scrophularia'' are derived from a different species, ''[[Scrophularia nodosa]]'', which has tubers amongst its roots which somewhat resemble [[Mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis|scrofulas]] and so were used as a treatment for this disease. The specific names "green figwort" and "''oblongifolia''" are self-evident, but the old name for this plant, ''S. umbrosa'' is more interesting, meaning "shady figwort".<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref>

==Identification==
Green figwort is very similar to the much commoner [[Scrophularia auriculata|water figwort]], which is why it was overlooked by botanists for so long. Differences include the leaf shape (sometimes lobed in water figwort), the teeth on the leaf margin (blunter in water figwort), and the shape of the staminode, which is bilobed in green figwort vs. entire in water figwort.<ref name="Stace" />
[[File:Scrophularia umbrosa subsp. umbrosa sl1.jpg|thumb|Close-ups of the staminode]]

==Distribution and status==
Green figwort is native to Europe and western Asia, as far north as the [[Baltic states]] and eastward to [[Xinjiang]]. It does not occur in Africa and in Sweden it is considered to be a recent introduction. It is not otherwise recorded as an introduction outside its natural range.<ref name="kew"/> There are old records of a figwort, either green- or water-figwort (accounts differ), as a casual in harbours in New York and Pennsylvania in the 19th century, but it did not persist.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scrophularia - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Scrophularia |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=floranorthamerica.org}}</ref>

In Britain there are distinct several areas where green figwort is quite common. These are centred on several major river basins, such as the lower Severn in Worcestershire and neighbouring counties. Possibly the first British record is from this area, in 1848, when it was found by J.H. Thompson beside the Sapey Brook.<ref name=Maskew>{{Cite book |last=Maskew |first=Roger |title=The Flora of Worcestershire |publisher=Roger Maskew |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-9926693-0-0 |location=Stoke Bliss}}</ref> Other centres of distribution include the valleys of the [[River Yare]] in Norfolk, the [[River Ribble|Ribble]] in Yorkshire, the [[River Eden, Cumbria| Eden in Cumbria]] and the [[River Tweed|Tweed]] in Scotland.<ref name="Perring">{{cite book |last1=Perring |first1=F.H. | last2=Walters |first2=S.M. |title=Atlas of the British Flora |date=1962 |publisher=Thomas Nelson and Sons Ltd. |location=Edinburgh}}</ref>

The global conservation status of this species, as of 2013, is [[Least-concern species|Least Concern]],<ref>[https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/19620681/19620926 IUCN - Scrophularia umbrosa]</ref> as it is in Britain and France.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scrofulaire à feuilles oblongues |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/122029 |access-date=20 December 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref> In Ireland, however, it is much rarer and considered to be Near Threatened in the [[Republic of Ireland|Republic]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Red Lists {{!}} National Parks & Wildlife Service |url=https://www.npws.ie/publications/red-lists |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=www.npws.ie}}</ref> and protected under Schedule 8 of the Wildlife (Northern Ireland) Order in the [[Northern Ireland|north]].<ref>{{Cite web |others=Expert Participation |title=The Wildlife (Northern Ireland) Order 1985 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1985/171/contents |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240624091434/https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1985/171/contents |archive-date=2024-06-24 |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=www.legislation.gov.uk |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>[https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/scrophularia-umbrosa Online Atlas of British and Irish Flora - ''Scrophularia umbrosa'']</ref> It is considered an [[axiophyte]] in any British county.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
The habitat of green figwort is on the edge of ditches in farmland and small streams through woods, where it trails over other plants rather than growing erect. It is found in swamps of sedges such as [[Carex otrubae|false fox-sedge]] or in light woodland, typically slightly calcareous [[British NVC community W8|W8]] [[Fraxinus excelsior|ash]] woodland in Britain.<ref name="Lockton" />
Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 9, R = 7, N = 7, and S = 0, which describe its habitat as semi-open, very wet, with a neutral pH and moderate fertility; but no salt.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=18 December 2024}}</ref> It is often found growing with [[Scrophularia auriculata|water figwort]], [[Scirpus sylvaticus|wood clubrush]], [[Lysimachia vulgaris|yellow loosestrife]] and [[Oenanthe crocata|hemlock water-dropwort]].<ref name=Sinker>{{Cite book |last1=Sinker |first1=C.A. |title=Ecological Flora of the Shropshire Region |last2=Packham |first2=J.R. |last3=Trueman |first3=I.C |last4=Oswald |first4=P.H. |last5=Perring |first5=F.H. |last6=Prestwood |first6=W.V. |publisher=Shropshire Wildlife Trust |year=1985 |isbn=0 95086 371 8 |location=Shrewsbury}}</ref><ref name="Maskew"/>

Plants are often infected with the rust ''[[Uromyces scrophulariae]]'' <small>(DC.) Fuckel (1870)</small>, which produces marks and distortions at the base of the stem.<ref name=redfern>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207-531 |isbn=1 85153 214 5}}</ref>

In Britain, the beetles ''[[Longitarsus agilis]]'' and ''L. nigrofasciatus'', and the sawfly ''[[Tenthredo scrophulariae]]'' are phytophagous on the leaves, whereas ''[[Cionus hortulanus]]'' eats the fruits and flowers as well. There is also a small fly called ''[[Contarinia|Contarinia scrophulariae]]'' which creates galls in the flower buds.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BRC - Database of Insects and their Food Plants |url=https://dbif.brc.ac.uk/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=5121 |access-date=2024-12-21 |website=dbif.brc.ac.uk}}</ref> In Europe, there are many more pests recorded on this species.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scrophularia umbrosa – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superasterids/asterids/lamiids/lamiales/scrophulariaceae/scrophularia/scrophularia-umbrosa/ |access-date=2024-12-21 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>

There is no information on the toxicity of green figwort specifically, but the closely related [[Scrophularia auriculata|water figwort]] has been reported to cause sickness in young cattle that ate it, and the same might well be true of green figwort.<ref name=poison>{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=M.R. |last2=Johnson |first2=A.W. |last3=Dauncey |first3=E.A. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi |date=2003 |publisher=The Stationery Office |location=London |isbn=0-11-702861-4}}</ref>

It is pollinated by bees and wasps.<ref>[http://www.ibiblio.org/pfaf/cgi-bin/arr_html?Scrophularia+umbrosa Plants for Life database]</ref>
